planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade; Joy Skies tolerates more sun than many shade perennials but still prefers protection from hot afternoon exposure.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil; Joy Skies is a navelwort selection bearing sprays of small, vivid blue, forget-me-not-like flowers over mounded, heart-shaped foliage in spring. It makes a good edging or woodland-border companion to hellebores and hostas, filling in before larger shade perennials reach full size. Keep soil evenly moist through the bloom period, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in shade to part shade; Moonlight's neon-bright chartreuse foliage colors up best out of direct sun.

directions: Plant in shade to part shade in humus-rich, evenly moist soil; Moonlight is a toad lily selection valued for its neon-bright chartreuse foliage, a striking foliage-color departure from the plain green leaves of most toad lily cultivars. Small purple-flecked white, orchid-like flowers appear along the upper stems in late summer and fall, true to the genus's typical autumn display. Grow it as a bright accent in a shaded border where its foliage color can stand out against darker companion plantings, and keep soil consistently moist through the growing season.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; Koji tolerates drier shade once established, like other Epimedium grandiflorum selections.

directions: Plant in partial shade to shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil; Koji bears large, pastel-toned flowers held on pale apple-green stems in early spring just above the emerging heart-shaped foliage. Like other Epimedium grandiflorum selections it tolerates dry shade and root competition from nearby trees once established, making it a reliable groundcover for a woodland garden's drier pockets. Trim back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flower stems emerge, to show off the spring bloom without last year's tattered leaves in the way.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade; Purple Pixie's vivid flower color shows up well against the dark shade-garden backdrop it's best planted in.

directions: Plant in shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil; Purple Pixie bears vivid purple sepals paired with long, extended white spurs on its spring flowers, one of the more boldly colored barrenwort selections. It forms a compact clump of heart-shaped foliage that provides season-long groundcover texture after the brief but showy spring bloom finishes. Like other Epimedium grandiflorum selections it tolerates dry shade and competition from tree roots once established, needing little supplemental water beyond the first growing season.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall into humus-rich, moist, well-drained woodland soil in shade; like other Trillium grandiflorum selections, Snowy White is slow to establish and best left undisturbed once planted.

directions: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall into humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained woodland soil in shade; Snowy White bears pure white, three-petaled flowers with wavy, curved-back petal edges in spring, a classic spring-ephemeral display before the tree canopy fully leafs out. Like all Trillium grandiflorum selections it is slow-growing and resents disturbance, so site it in a permanent woodland-garden location where it can be left undisturbed for years to naturalize. Avoid picking the flowers or leaves, since removing foliage can seriously set back or kill the plant by cutting off its only means of recharging the underground rhizome.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; like other Helleborus x ballardiae selections, HGC Diva holds its marbled evergreen foliage through winter.

directions: Plant in partial to full shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil; HGC Diva belongs to the Helleborus x ballardiae Gold Collection, a group of hybrid hellebores known for marbled or silvery-veined evergreen foliage and outward-facing winter-to-early-spring flowers that show up better than the downward-nodding blooms of older hellebore types. Like its Gold Collection siblings it is vigorous and floriferous, holding attractive foliage through winter in all but the harshest climates. Give it a permanent shaded spot with rich, well-drained soil, since established hellebores resent being moved.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Sun Flare belongs to the Winter Jewels strain, grown from seed rather than division, so individual plants vary slightly.

directions: Plant in partial to full shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil; Sun Flare is part of the Winter Jewels strain of Lenten rose, bred by Marietta and Ernie O'Byrne of Northwest Garden Nursery, bearing large, pale-yellow-to-golden-yellow double flowers in late winter and early spring over leathery evergreen foliage. As a seed strain rather than a clonally propagated cultivar, individual plants show some natural variation in flower form, which collectors often find part of the appeal. Give it a permanent shaded site with rich, well-drained soil, since mature hellebores resent transplanting.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade; Flash is a named selection of the shrubby East African impatiens, grown as a perennial in mild climates or an annual elsewhere.

directions: Plant in partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Flash is a selection of the large, shrubby East African species Impatiens sodenii, bearing snow-white blooms brushed with pink painterly strokes nearly year-round in mild climates. Unlike bedding impatiens, this species grows into a substantial woody-based shrub reaching 4-6 feet, earning it the common name poor man's rhododendron for its scale and continuous flowering. It is frost-tender and best grown as a perennial in zones 9-11 or as a large container specimen brought indoors for winter elsewhere, needing consistent moisture and rich soil to sustain its near-constant bloom.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-enriched soil in bright shade; this collected form from Jeju Island, South Korea shares the species' carefree, low-maintenance habit.

directions: Plant in bright shade in moist, humus-enriched soil; Cheju-Do is a collected form of Japanese bugbane named for Jeju Island (formerly Cheju-do), South Korea, carrying the species' lush, layered, jagged-edged glossy green leaves. Small white bottlebrush flower spikes rise above the foliage mound in late summer, a modest but welcome bonus on top of the handsome foliage display. It is a carefree, low-maintenance woodland perennial once established in consistently moist, humus-rich soil, needing little attention beyond an annual mulch top-up.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Amethyst Summer blooms over a long season from summer into fall with deadheading.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil; Amethyst Summer bears mauve-suffused rich pink bottlebrush flower spikes continuously from early summer into fall over mounded, arrow-shaped foliage. Like other Persicaria amplexicaulis selections it tolerates considerable shade while still flowering well, making it a versatile filler for a part-shade border or pond margin where consistent moisture is available. It spreads gradually by rhizome to form a substantial clump over a few seasons; divide in spring if it outgrows its space.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Anne's Choice is one of the brighter-flowered fleeceflower selections, blooming heavily from summer into fall.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil; Anne's Choice is a bright red-flowered fleeceflower selection, producing dense bottlebrush spikes continuously from early summer well into fall over mounded, arrow-shaped foliage. It tolerates considerable shade while still flowering reliably, making it a useful long-season color source for a part-shade border or pond-edge planting. It spreads gradually by rhizome, forming a substantial clump within a few seasons; divide congested clumps in spring to keep it in bounds and share with other beds.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Fat Domino's notably thick flower spikes give it a bolder presence in the border than finer-textured fleeceflower selections.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil; Fat Domino bears unusually thick, dark red flower spikes shot through with purplish overtones, giving it a bolder, chunkier presence than finer-textured fleeceflower cultivars. Flowering runs continuously from early summer into fall over mounded, arrow-shaped foliage, and the plant tolerates considerable shade while still blooming well. It spreads by rhizome to form a substantial clump over a few seasons, making it a good anchor plant for a part-shade border or damp pond margin.
